---
title: "File Types, File Sizes, and Storage"
---

## Why this matters

RNA-seq analysis creates many files. Some are small text files that describe your samples. Others are large sequencing, alignment, or intermediate files that can quickly use hundreds of gigabytes.

Before running a pipeline, it helps to know:

- Which files are inputs
- Which files are outputs
- Which files are temporary
- Which files need to be saved
- Which files can be deleted later

## Common file types

| File type | Example | What it is |
|---|---|---|
| FASTQ | `sample_R1.fastq.gz` | Raw sequencing reads |
| CSV | `samplesheet.csv` | Table describing samples and input files |
| FASTA | `genome.fa` | Reference genome or transcript sequences |
| GTF/GFF | `annotation.gtf` | Gene annotation file |
| BAM | `sample.bam` | Aligned reads |
| BAI | `sample.bam.bai` | Index for a BAM file |
| TSV/CSV | `salmon.merged.gene_counts.tsv` | Count or expression table |
| HTML | `multiqc_report.html` | Interactive report opened in a browser |
| LOG/TXT | `.nextflow.log` | Logs and command output |

## FASTQ files

FASTQ files are usually the main input for RNA-seq pipelines.

Paired-end data often has two files per sample:

```text
sample1_R1.fastq.gz
sample1_R2.fastq.gz
```

The file names usually tell you:

- The sample name
- Whether the file is read 1 (`R1`) or read 2 (`R2`)
- Whether the file is compressed (`.gz`)

FASTQ files can be large. A single compressed FASTQ file may be several gigabytes.

## Reference files

Reference files describe the genome or transcriptome you want to compare your reads against.

Common reference files include:

```text
genome.fa
annotation.gtf
```

For non-model organisms like *Staurois parvus*, reference files may come from a lab assembly or a closely related species, depending on the project.

::: {.callout-note}
The choice of reference affects the interpretation of RNA-seq results. Always record which genome and annotation files were used.
:::

## Pipeline outputs

nf-core pipelines create organized output folders. The exact files depend on the options you choose, but common outputs include:

- Quality-control reports
- Quantification tables
- Alignment files
- Pipeline logs
- Software version files
- MultiQC summary reports

The most useful output to open first is usually:

```text
multiqc_report.html
```

## Temporary files

Nextflow creates a work directory that stores intermediate files:

```text
work/
```

This folder can become very large. It is useful while the pipeline is running and if you need to resume a failed run.

After the analysis is complete and you are sure you do not need to resume, the `work/` directory can often be deleted to save space.

::: {.callout-warning}
Do not delete `work/` while a pipeline is running. Do not delete it before confirming that your final outputs were created successfully.
:::

## Typical storage needs

Exact storage needs depend on the number of samples, read depth, reference files, and pipeline options.

As a rough guide:

| Project size | Input FASTQs | Suggested scratch space |
|---|---:|---:|
| Small test run | Less than 5 GB | 30 GB |
| Small project | 10-50 GB | 100-300 GB |
| Medium project | 50-200 GB | 300 GB-1 TB |
| Large project | More than 200 GB | 1 TB or more |

For this tutorial, we create a workspace with 30 GB because it is meant for a small demo.

## Check file sizes

To see the size of files and folders in your current directory, run:

```bash
du -sh *
```

Example output:

```text
4.2G    data
18G     work
2.1G    results
8.0K    samplesheet.csv
```

To check free space in a filesystem, run:

```bash
df -h .
```

Example output:

```text
Filesystem      Size  Used Avail Use% Mounted on
workspace        30G   24G  6.0G  80% /scratch4/workspace
```

## What should you keep?

Usually keep:

- `samplesheet.csv`
- Final results folder
- MultiQC report
- Count or expression tables
- Pipeline information files
- Exact commands and parameters used

Usually do not keep forever:

- Large temporary `work/` files
- Failed test outputs
- Duplicate downloaded references
- Old intermediate files that can be regenerated

## Good habits

- Use clear folder names
- Keep raw data separate from results
- Record where files came from
- Do not edit raw FASTQ files
- Check available space before starting a large run
- Clean up temporary files after confirming final results

::: {.callout-tip}
When in doubt, ask before deleting large files. It is much easier to delete temporary files later than to recover important data after it is gone.
:::
